processing: Not a single recipe: this provincial brand spans several tea classes. The green tea is made in the usual way for Chinese greens, fixed, shaped and dried into straight buds.
harvest_season: Varies by producer; as with other Sichuan greens, spring tea is the one prized.
appearance_dry: The green style is straight and neat, tender green and even.
appearance_liquor: The green style gives a bright, tender green cup.
appearance_wet: Little is documented; expect tender green buds and leaves in the green style.
taste_profile: The green style is described as mellow and brisk with a sweet return and a lasting chestnut aroma.

brewing.notes: For the green style only. Black and other classes sold under the name need their own treatment, so check the class first.

vintage_note: The name alone does not tell you the class or the age. The green tea is sold as the current harvest, as usual for Sichuan greens; other classes follow their own norms, so read the producer and harvest date on the pack.
description:
Tianfu Longya is less one tea than a Sichuan provincial brand, used by a group of tea companies across the province. The green is the usual meaning, but the same name also covers black and other classes.

Growing areas are described in broad terms: the hills around the rim of the Sichuan basin and the basin's own low hills. That breadth matters, because two packs may share little beyond the name.

The green style is described as neat, straight tender leaf with a bright cup, a mellow brisk taste and a chestnut aroma. The black style is reported as fine, tight, gold-tipped leaf with a citrus-candy scent.

When buying, treat the producer as the real information. Check the class, the county and the harvest date on the pack.
history: Little is documented about this name as a tea rather than as a brand. It belongs to the recent push to give Sichuan tea a stronger shared identity, and it is listed among the province's well-known teas today.
